introduction_markdown: Answer ALL questions. Section I is designed to be answered in 1 hour and Section II in 1½ hours. You are advised to divide your time accordingly. In Section II answer EITHER parts a, b and c OR parts d, e and f of each question (Section II: answer ALL questions, choosing one question from each pair of alternatives). For your guidance the approximate mark for each part of a question is indicated in brackets. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Where necessary, assume: the acceleration of free fall, $g = 10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$; the speed of light in air, $c = 3\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the charge on an electron, $e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$. Calculators are allowed.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) A polythene rod can be charged by rubbing. Identify the type of charge acquired by the rod and explain its origin. *[2 marks]*

Two charged metallic balls A and B on insulating stands are placed a short distance from each other as shown in figure 3. Ball A is positively charged while ball B is negatively charged.

![fig-1](gce-ol-physics-2021-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_9_fig_1.png)

*Figure 3*

(ii) Name the type of force that exist between A and B. *[1 mark]*

(iii) State two factors that affect the size of the force. *[2 marks]*

(iv) State and explain what will happen if A and B are connected using a conducting wire. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) The polythene rod acquires a **negative charge**. When it is rubbed with a cloth, electrons are transferred by friction from the cloth to the rod. The rod then has an excess of electrons (negative) while the cloth, which has lost electrons, becomes positively charged.

(ii) An **attractive electrostatic force**, because A and B carry opposite charges (unlike charges attract).

(iii) The size of the force depends on (any two): the **magnitudes of the charges** on the balls (the larger the charges, the larger the force); the **distance between the balls** (the force decreases as the distance increases); the medium between them.

(iv) Electrons flow through the conducting wire from the negatively charged ball B to the positively charged ball A, until the charges are neutralised (if the charges are equal in magnitude both balls become neutral; otherwise the remaining charge is shared so that both balls are at the same potential). The balls are then discharged, so the force between them disappears (or becomes zero) and they no longer attract each other.

questions.enonce_markdown:
A battery causes charges to move round a circuit for $30\,\mathrm{s}$ and it is observed that the current in the circuit is $5\,\mathrm{A}$. Calculate:

(i) the quantity of charge that passes through the battery. *[2 marks]*

(ii) the number of electrons that flow round the circuit per unit time given that the charge on one electron is $1.6\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$. *[2 marks]*

(iii) the amount of energy converted into heat and light by a lamp, given that this battery provides a p.d. of $12\,\mathrm{V}$ across the lamp. *[2 marks]*

(iv) Differentiate between the potential difference (p.d.) the battery can supply across an external load such as a lamp and the electromotive force (e.m.f.) of the battery. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) $Q = It = 5\times 30 = 150\,\mathrm{C}$.

(ii) The charge flowing per second is $I = 5\,\mathrm{C\,s^{-1}}$. Number of electrons per second:

$\dfrac{N}{t} = \dfrac{I}{e} = \dfrac{5}{1.6\times10^{-19}} = 3.1\times10^{19}\ \text{electrons per second}$.

(iii) Energy $W = QV = 150\times 12 = 1800\,\mathrm{J}$ (equivalently $W = VIt = 12\times 5\times 30$).

(iv) The **e.m.f.** is the total energy supplied by the battery to each coulomb of charge passing through it (the energy converted from chemical to electrical form per unit charge), measured when no current is drawn. The **p.d.** across an external load is the energy converted to other forms in the load per unit charge. The p.d. across the lamp is less than the e.m.f. when a current flows, because some energy per coulomb is used to drive the charge through the internal resistance of the battery ($V = E - Ir$).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Draw a ring circuit used in house wiring. Your diagram should clearly show how a socket carrying a fuse is connected to the ring circuit. *[3 marks]*

(ii) State two advantages of the ring circuit over a linear circuit. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) **Ring circuit diagram** (described): the consumer unit (fuse box or circuit breaker) at the source is drawn with three terminals: live (L), neutral (N) and earth (E). A **live wire** leaves the live terminal, runs in a closed loop round the house passing close to each socket, and returns to the same live terminal; the **neutral wire** and the **earth wire** form similar loops from and back to their own terminals. Each socket is connected **in parallel** across the ring, its live pin taken from the live loop, its neutral pin from the neutral loop and its earth pin from the earth loop. A **fuse** (for example $13\,\mathrm{A}$) is placed in the live connection of the plug of each socket; the ring itself is protected by a larger fuse or circuit breaker (about $30\,\mathrm{A}$) at the consumer unit.

(ii) Advantages of the ring circuit (any two): the current reaches each socket by two paths, so each wire carries only about half of the current, and thinner (cheaper) cable can be used; the voltage drop is smaller, so appliances get nearly the full voltage; a larger number of sockets can be supplied and added easily; if the wire breaks at one point, the supply to all sockets is maintained through the other path.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Differentiate between soft and hard magnetic materials. *[2 marks]*

Two bar magnets are placed side by side as shown in figure 4.

![fig-2](gce-ol-physics-2021-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_9_fig_2.png)

*Figure 4*

(ii) Name the type of force that exists between the two magnets. *[1 mark]*

(iii) Name two factors that affect the size of the force. *[2 marks]*

(iv) Copy the diagram and draw the magnetic field pattern between the two magnets. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) A **soft magnetic material** (for example soft iron) is easily magnetised and loses its magnetism easily when the magnetising field is removed; it is used for electromagnets and transformer cores. A **hard magnetic material** (for example steel) is difficult to magnetise but keeps its magnetism for a long time; it is used to make permanent magnets.

(ii) A **repulsive force**: the two facing ends are both south poles, and like poles repel.

(iii) The size of the force depends on (any two): the **strength of the magnets** (pole strengths) and the **distance between** the two magnets (the force decreases as the distance increases).

(iv) **Field pattern** (described): copy the two bars with their poles. Magnetic field lines leave the north pole of each magnet and enter its south pole, with arrows pointing away from N and towards S. Between the two facing south poles the lines coming from the two sides **do not join and do not cross**: they curve away from each other on either side of the gap, each set of lines bending round into its own south pole. In the middle of the gap there is a **neutral point** where the magnetic field is zero (no lines pass through it), and the lines are drawn closest together near the poles, where the field is strongest.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 4 shows a transformer used to operate a radio set.

![fig-3](gce-ol-physics-2021-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_9_fig_3.png)

*Figure 4*

Calculate:

(i) the output voltage using the figures on the diagram. *[2 marks]*

(ii) the current in the primary coil given that the current in the secondary coil is $2\,\mathrm{A}$, assuming that the efficiency of the transformer is $100\,\%$. *[2 marks]*

(iii) the power of the radio set. *[2 marks]*

(iv) State two sources of energy losses in a transformer. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
From the figure: primary voltage $V_p = 240\,\mathrm{V}$ on $N_p = 1000$ turns; secondary (radio set) on $N_s = 100$ turns.

(i) $\dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p}$, so $V_s = 240\times\dfrac{100}{1000} = 24\,\mathrm{V}$.

(ii) For a $100\,\%$ efficient transformer, power in = power out: $V_pI_p = V_sI_s$, so

$I_p = \dfrac{V_sI_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{24\times 2}{240} = 0.2\,\mathrm{A}$.

(iii) Power of the radio set $P = V_sI_s = 24\times 2 = 48\,\mathrm{W}$.

(iv) Energy losses (any two): the **resistance of the copper windings** (heating, $I^2R$); **eddy currents** in the iron core (reduced by laminating the core); **hysteresis** losses (repeated magnetisation and demagnetisation of the core); **flux leakage** (not all the flux of the primary links the secondary); sound/vibration.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 5 shows a solenoid XY with a current flowing in the direction indicated.

![fig-4](gce-ol-physics-2021-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_9_fig_4.png)

*Figure 5*

(i) Copy the diagram and indicate the magnetic flux pattern around the solenoid. *[3 marks]*

(ii) State two factors that will affect the strength of the magnetic field. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) **Flux pattern** (described): the field of a solenoid is like that of a bar magnet. Inside the solenoid the magnetic field lines are **straight, parallel to the axis and evenly spaced** (a uniform field). Outside, the lines are closed loops which leave the solenoid at one end, curve round and enter at the other end, spreading out far from the coil. With the current direction shown (downwards on the front of the turns), the right-hand grip rule gives: end **Y is the north pole** (the lines emerge there) and end **X is the south pole** (the lines enter there). The arrows therefore point from X to Y inside the solenoid and from Y round to X outside.

(ii) The strength of the magnetic field increases with (any two): a **larger current** in the coil; a **larger number of turns** per unit length; the presence of a **soft-iron core** inside the solenoid.
